lead: Indiana homes deal with river floods, severe storms and winter freezes. DryBeacon helps owners from Indianapolis to Evansville get water out and drying started.
risk: severe storms and tornadoes, river flooding and frozen pipes
why: Most of Indiana's FEMA disasters since 2000 came from severe storms. Strong wind and hail damage roofs, then rain gets in. In June 2008, floods hit Columbus, Franklin and other central Indiana towns hard. The Ohio, Wabash and White rivers still flood homes in wet springs.

Basements are common, and so are sump pumps. When the power fails in a storm, the pump stops and water rises. Over half of Indiana homes were built before 1980, so old drain lines and water heaters fail often. Illinois and Ohio share these risks.
image_alt: Home surrounded by water after a heavy rain storm
image_caption: Heavy spring rain and river flooding put water around Indiana homes in low areas.
problems: Ohio, Wabash and White river towns
tips: Add a battery backup or water-powered backup to your sump pump.
Point downspouts at least six feet from the house.
Shut off outside faucets before winter.
Keep a wet-dry vacuum handy for small basement leaks.
insurance: Sump pump failure is often excluded unless you buy a water backup endorsement, which many Indiana insurers offer.

faq.q: What do I do if my sump pump fails during a storm?
faq.a: Stay out of standing water if outlets or cords are wet. Turn off power to the basement if you can do it safely. Then call DryBeacon to pump out the water and start drying before mold grows.
